concepts.name: administrative research
concepts.short: In Lazarsfeld’s 1941 distinction, communication research with empirical methods that serves the practical aims of a particular institution.

concepts.name: agenda-setting
concepts.short: The idea that the emphasis the news media give to issues influences how important the public considers those issues: the media shape not what people think, but what they think about.

concepts.name: broadcasting
concepts.short: Sending the same programme from a centre to a large number of receivers at the same time; the basic form of radio and television.

concepts.name: climate of opinion
concepts.short: The perception of which opinion is widespread, rising or in favour around one on an issue. In the spiral of silence, this perception rather than the real distribution shapes behaviour.

concepts.name: the three social functions of communication
concepts.short: The three jobs communication does for society, according to Lasswell: surveillance of the environment, correlating the parts of society in their response, and transmitting the social heritage across generations.

concepts.name: communication
concepts.short: The process in which people try to convey or share meaning through symbols. It has no single definition: some definitions stress the transmission of a message, others the building of shared meaning.

concepts.name: critical research
concepts.short: In Lazarsfeld’s 1941 distinction, communication research that questions, on the basis of values, the media’s general role in society and the problems beneath it.

concepts.name: cultivation theory
concepts.short: Gerbner’s theory that heavy television viewers’ perception of social reality is closer to the recurring messages of the on-screen world than that of similar light viewers; it sees the effect as accumulation spread over years.

concepts.name: Cultural Indicators Project
concepts.short: A long-running research programme that George Gerbner started in the late 1960s, monitoring television content over the years and combining it with viewer surveys; the framework of cultivation theory.

concepts.name: entropy
concepts.short: Shannon’s measure of information: the number, in bits, that shows how much freedom of choice a source has among possible messages.

concepts.name: falsifiability
concepts.short: That a theory could turn out incompatible with some possible observation; for Popper, the criterion separating scientific from non-scientific theory.

concepts.name: fear of isolation
concepts.short: Fear of being excluded, of falling out of one’s surroundings’ favour. In the spiral of silence, the engine that drives people to probe the climate of opinion and to fall silent when they sense they are in the minority.

concepts.name: gatekeeping
concepts.short: The selection process that determines whether a story or piece of information passes through a media channel; the first link in the formation of the media agenda.

concepts.name: hard core
concepts.short: The minority that is not caught in the spiral and goes on defending its opinion, accepting exclusion (or because it is already excluded). Noelle-Neumann adds the “avant-garde” beside it.

concepts.name: heavy viewers
concepts.short: The upper end of the grouping by amount of television viewing in cultivation research; on the other side of the comparison are light viewers (those who watch little).

concepts.name: Lasswell’s formula
concepts.short: A way of describing an act of communication through five questions: who says what, in which channel, to whom, with what effect? Each question corresponds to a field of research.

concepts.name: linear transmission model
concepts.short: An approach that sees communication as a one-way transfer of a message from sender to receiver. Lasswell and Shannon–Weaver count as its first examples; it is most often criticised as having “no feedback, no context, no meaning”.

concepts.name: hypodermic needle (magic bullet) model
concepts.short: The textbook story that mass media deliver messages directly and uniformly to a passive, isolated audience, like an injection or a bullet that hits its target; according to historians, a label added later.

concepts.name: mainstreaming
concepts.short: The way heavy television viewing erodes differences in outlook that stem from factors such as age, education and political orientation and brings people closer to a common “television mainstream”.

concepts.name: mass communication
concepts.short: A form of communication in which messages reach a dispersed audience through technical means, publicly, indirectly and one-way; the communicator is usually an institution.

concepts.name: mass media
concepts.short: Print, electronic and digital channels that carry the same message at the same time to large numbers of people who do not know one another and are scattered.

concepts.name: mean world syndrome
concepts.short: Heavy television viewers seeing the world as more dangerous, insecure and mean than it really is; the best-known concept of Gerbner’s cultivation work.

concepts.name: media agenda
concepts.short: The ordering of issues by importance in newspapers, bulletins and websites: which issue gets how much space, airtime and priority.

concepts.name: media-centric
concepts.short: A view that grants media and communication autonomy and influence of their own and treats media as a driver of social change (McQuail).

concepts.name: message system analysis
concepts.short: The second prong of Cultural Indicators: systematically counting and tracking recurring patterns in media content (who appears, what they do, what they do to whom).

concepts.name: metacommunication
concepts.short: Communication about communication: cues about how a message is to be understood and how the two parties relate. For Watzlawick, the relationship aspect of communication classifies its content aspect.

concepts.name: middle-range theory
concepts.short: A testable theory of a delimited domain, standing between small working hypotheses and large theories that aim to explain everything at once.

concepts.name: movable type
concepts.short: Making each character a separate piece so that it can be set into a page, printed and then reused; developed in clay, wood and metal in different parts of the world.

concepts.name: need for orientation
concepts.short: A concept that predicts a person’s wish to turn to the news media on an issue: the combination of personal relevance and uncertainty. It explains in whom agenda-setting will be stronger.

concepts.name: news agency
concepts.short: An organization that gathers news and sells it to many newspapers and broadcasters; with the telegraph it sped up the turning of news into a commercial product in the 19th century.

concepts.name: noise
concepts.short: In Shannon’s diagram, everything added to the signal during transmission that the source did not intend (static, distortion, errors). Weaver also proposed “semantic noise”, which distorts meaning.

concepts.name: nonverbal communication
concepts.short: Communication through everything other than words, such as facial expression, gesture, posture, tone of voice and distance; it works together with verbal communication and often complements it.

concepts.name: paradigm
concepts.short: In Kuhn, the exemplary achievements a scientific community shares, together with the beliefs, values and tools that go with them; in communication studies often used loosely for a “dominant approach”.

concepts.name: penny press
concepts.short: A type of newspaper that appeared in American cities in the 1830s: sold on the street for one cent, financed by advertising and turning to local and human-interest news.

concepts.name: powerful effects assumption
concepts.short: The belief that media can shape public opinion, attitudes and behaviour strongly; it recurs in different forms from the propaganda worry of the 1920s–30s to Noelle-Neumann (1973) and mid-range theories, and is not one single theory.

concepts.name: priming
concepts.short: An issue or area that stands out in the media becoming the yardstick people use when judging a leader or an event.

concepts.name: public agenda
concepts.short: The ranking of the issues that the public (or a sample) considers important; usually measured by survey.

concepts.name: public opinion
concepts.short: In the spiral of silence, public opinion is not a voting total but a means of social control: the opinions a person can express openly without being excluded, or must openly show in order not to be excluded.

concepts.name: quasi-statistical sense
concepts.short: According to Noelle-Neumann, an almost statistician-like “sixth sense” that lets people, without running a poll, sense which opinion is rising and which is declining around them.

concepts.name: resonance
concepts.short: When everyday life experience and television messages overlap, the cultivation effect gets a “double dose” and becomes stronger.

concepts.name: ritual view
concepts.short: The view that sees communication less as carrying information and more as sharing, participation and community, focused on representing and maintaining shared beliefs. It is the view James W. Carey proposed against the transmission view.

concepts.name: salience
concepts.short: How far an issue, person or attribute stands out on an agenda; that is, its perceived importance. In agenda-setting this is what is transferred from the media to the public.

concepts.name: second-level agenda-setting
concepts.short: The idea that the media transfer to the public not only which issues, but also which attributes of issues or persons stand out.

concepts.name: Shannon–Weaver model
concepts.short: An engineering theory that draws a communication system as source, transmitter, channel, receiver and destination (plus a noise source) and focuses on measuring how accurately a message is carried.

concepts.name: society-centric
concepts.short: A view that sees the media mainly as a reflection of political and economic forces and media theory as a special application of broader social theory (McQuail).

concepts.name: spiral of silence
concepts.short: People sense which opinion is gaining strength around them; those left in the minority fall silent out of fear of isolation, which makes their opinion look weaker than it is, and the process accelerates like a spiral. Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann’s theory.

concepts.name: suggestibility
concepts.short: A person’s tendency to accept incoming information as true without testing it enough. Cantril explained it in his Mars study through “standards of judgment” and “checking up”; the concept reaches back to the suggestion doctrine of the early twentieth century.

concepts.name: theory
concepts.short: A systematic set of ideas that helps make sense of a phenomenon, explain it, predict a consequence and guide action; in the strict sense, connected propositions from which observed regularities can be derived.

concepts.name: transmission view
concepts.short: The view that sees communication as the sending of messages over distance, the carrying of information from one place to another. One of the two views that Carey contrasts with each other.

concepts.name: Weaver’s three levels
concepts.short: Three layers of communication problems: A technical (how accurately are symbols transmitted), B semantic (how well does meaning arrive), C effectiveness (how far does received meaning affect conduct).
